Cross-platform malware changes the assumption that one operating system is the attacker’s destination.  Modern languages and shared code bases make it easier to adapt malicious tooling across Windows, Linux, and virtualization environments. For infrastructure teams, that means endpoint security cannot be planned as a collection of isolated platform problems.  The control plane, identity plane, servers, developer systems, and user endpoints increasingly belong in the same threat model.  In practical terms, it is a good time to: • Compare endpoint detection coverage across Windows, Linux, and server workloads. • Identify privileged identities shared across administrative environments. • Review Conditional Access policies for administrator access to cloud control planes. • Audit service principals and workload identities with cross-environment privileges. • Test incident-response handoffs between endpoint, cloud, and infrastructure teams.  #CloudSecurity #CyberResilience #IdentitySecurity #SecurityOperations csoonline.com/article/399738…

The most fearless animal on Earth just handed its life to something the size of a coffee mug. Not out of kindness. Out of arithmetic. Watch the video first. Sound on. Then come back, because what you just saw is the oldest business model on the planet, and almost nobody notices the deal being signed. Here is what no wildlife documentary tells you: this is not a story about courage, cuteness or survival. It is a story about a contract with no lawyers, no currency and no way to enforce it. It has held for millions of years. It should have collapsed in a week. Let me show you why. 1/ The enemy that never makes the documentary A lion is an event. A tick is a lifestyle. Predators get the soundtrack, the slow motion, the narrator whispering. Parasites get the bodies. Across the African savanna, far more animals are quietly drained than are ever eaten. Start with the tick, because everything else in this thread bends around it. There are roughly 900 species. They have no wings, no jump, no speed. What they have is patience. A tick climbs a blade of grass, stretches its front legs into the air and waits. Days. Weeks. Some species can wait years between meals. It does not see you. It smells you. A cluster of sensors on its front legs, called the Haller's organ, reads carbon dioxide, body heat and the chemistry of sweat. The instant something warm brushes past, it grabs on. Then comes the part that should bother you. It does not just bite. It cuts a small channel, anchors itself with a glue-like cement, and injects saliva that works like a pharmacy: an anesthetic so you feel nothing, an anticoagulant so the blood keeps flowing, and compounds that quiet your immune response so your body does not fight back. You get bitten by something that has already turned off your alarm. It feeds for days. A female can swell to many times her starting weight, drop off, lay thousands of eggs, and die. The next generation is already waiting on the grass. For a wild animal, a heavy load is not an annoyance. It is anemia. Infection. Weakness at the exact moment weakness gets you killed. Ticks carry pathogens, and every animal on that savanna is an unwilling delivery route. Now the cruel detail, the one that makes the whole story possible: Ticks prefer the places an animal cannot reach. Head. Neck. Spine. Between the shoulder blades. Behind the ears. The patches where a tongue, a claw or a rough tree trunk cannot get a clean strike. Evolution gave every large animal a body that is a fortress in front and a buffet in back. Remember that. It matters in about two minutes. 2/ A body engineered to need nobody Meet the honey badger. Roughly 10 kilograms. An adult male lion is about twenty times heavier. On paper, this is a snack with attitude. In practice, Guinness has listed it as the most fearless animal in the world, and the reputation is earned. Look at the engineering. Its skin is thick and so loose that when a predator clamps down, the badger can twist inside its own skin and bite back. You cannot hold something that does not stay where you grabbed it. It raids beehives and eats the larvae while hundreds of bees sting it. It digs prey out of the ground, eats scorpions, tortoises and porcupines, and goes after venomous snakes as lunch. Field reports describe badgers bitten by cobras and puff adders who simply collapse, sleep it off for a couple of hours, wake up and finish the snake. There is a real scientific reason. In 2015, a paper in the journal Toxicon was literally titled "Why the honey badger don't care." The finding: a specific receptor in its muscles, the target of snake neurotoxins, has mutations that blunt the venom. Not magic. Molecular armor. And the badger is smart in a way that unsettles people. A captive honey badger named Stoffel at a South African rehabilitation centre became famous for escaping enclosures: stacking objects, using a rake, piling up mud, reading the geometry of the fence like an engineer who hates fences. Keepers kept raising the stakes. Stoffel kept raising the IQ. So here is an animal that has engineered away almost every form of dependence. No predator it truly needs to fear. No prey it cannot crack. No door it cannot open. And it still has one problem it cannot solve alone. The problem is on its back. 3/ The small ones Now the other side of the deal. The banded mongoose weighs under two kilograms. It lives in groups, usually ten to thirty animals, and it is one of the strangest social experiments in mammals. Female banded mongooses in a group often give birth on the same night. Not the same week. The same night, sometimes within hours of each other, in one shared den. Researchers who have followed these groups in Uganda for years describe it as a kind of reproductive lottery with the numbers deliberately scrambled: because nobody knows whose pup is whose, everyone has a reason to protect all of them. Each pup, once it leaves the den, pairs up with a single adult, an escort, that feeds it, defends it, and carries it out of trouble. Parenthood as a group project with individual contracts inside it. They also use tools, sort of. A banded mongoose finds an egg it cannot crack, turns its back to a hard surface, and hurls the egg between its hind legs against a rock. Blind aim. Perfect result. They forage in the open, in a pack, noses down, which should be suicide. It is not, because someone is always watching. Sentinels scan the horizon, and the group trades vigilance the way other animals trade food. And, like the badger, mongooses took the same evolutionary shortcut against snake venom. That 2015 paper found that honey badgers, mongooses, hedgehogs and pigs all arrived, independently, at the same fix for the same receptor. Four lineages. Same lock, same key, found separately. When evolution repeats itself that precisely, it is not a coincidence. It is a verdict. So you have two animals, both venom-proof, both unnervingly confident, both built by the same pressures. One is a solitary heavyweight with a bad temper. The other is a crowd. One has the strength. The other has the numbers. One cannot reach its own back. The other has a hundred small hands and an appetite. You see where this is going. You do not yet see why it should not work. 4/ The deal Here is the transaction, stripped to its bones: Party A has a problem it cannot reach. Party B is hungry, and the problem is food. That is it. No gratitude. No friendship. One animal's parasite is another animal's lunch, which makes the exchange the cleanest kind of trade there is: each side hands over the thing that is worthless to them and receives something that is worth everything. Biologists call it cleaning symbiosis, and it is far more common than most people realize. On coral reefs, a cleaner wrasse, a fish about the length of your finger, runs a roadside shop. Giant groupers, moray eels and even sharks line up to be inspected. By some estimates, a single cleaner wrasse serves well over a thousand client visits a day, picking off parasites, dead skin and mucus. The client holds still, flares its gills open, and lets a fish that could be swallowed in one bite work inside its mouth. On the savanna, the same pattern, different cast. Banded mongooses have long been documented climbing onto warthogs and picking off ticks. The warthog, a tusked, armored animal that fights lions and wins more often than you would expect, lies down and allows it. Then there are oxpeckers, birds that ride on buffalo, rhino and giraffe, eating ticks. For decades this was the textbook example of mutualism. Then researchers noticed that oxpeckers also drink blood from open wounds and may keep those wounds from healing. Is it a partnership or a polite parasite? The answer is still being argued. That argument matters, because it exposes the hidden question inside every one of these relationships: How do you know your partner is not cheating? 5/ The arithmetic of one meal Zoom in on a single transaction, because the numbers are stranger than the story. An engorged tick is not an insect snack. It is a balloon of someone else's blood. Days of feeding have turned a flat, seed-sized parasite into a swollen, grey-blue capsule packed with protein and fat, delivered without the cleaner ever having to cut through skin, chase prey or fight anything. For a small hunter, that is a ready-made meal sitting on a stationary buffet. Now do the host's math. A heavy tick load drains blood, spreads infection, and leaves open wounds that invite more infection. Remove a few dozen ticks and you remove a dozen small drains, a handful of potential disease routes, and a few days of the immune system's attention. The host does not need a perfect cleaning. It needs a good enough one, delivered for free, on exactly the places it cannot touch. Look at what each side actually pays. The cleaner pays time and exposure. It stands on top of an animal that could crush it, in open terrain, with its head down. The host pays time and exposure. It lies still, eyes half shut, with a stranger's claws on its spine. Neither pays in the currency that wildlife shows usually dramatize: blood, bone, territory, mates. The entire exchange runs on a resource that both sides produce in abundance and neither values: one animal's infestation, another animal's appetite. That is not a coincidence. That is how stable trade always works. The best deals are the ones where each party hands over what costs them nothing and receives what they could never get alone. Every durable economy, from a Roman olive market to a modern app store, rests on the same math. The savanna just got there first. 6/ Why it should collapse Think about the incentives for a moment, the way an economist or a cynic would. If you are the cleaner, the easiest meal is not the tick. The tick is small, hard to remove and requires patience. The easiest meal is the host itself: skin, blood, mucus. Take a bite of the client and you eat better, faster. If you are the host, the easiest move is not to wait for the cleaning to end. The host is bigger. The host is hungry. The cleaner is standing on its body, edible and defenseless. In game theory this is called the prisoner's dilemma, and the textbook answer is bleak: both sides defect, both sides lose. In the early 1980s, the political scientist Robert Axelrod ran computer tournaments to find the best strategy for repeated dilemmas. The winner was the simplest program entered. It cooperated on the first move, then copied whatever the other player did last. Tit for tat. Nice, retaliating, forgiving, clear. In 1971, years before Axelrod, the biologist Robert Trivers had used cleaner fish as a core example in his landmark paper on reciprocal altruism. His argument: cooperation between non-relatives can evolve if the same individuals meet again and again and cheating can be punished. That is what holds the whole structure together. Not trust. Repetition. The badger does not need to like the mongoose. It needs to see it tomorrow. Look at the enforcement tools nature built, because they are better than most legal systems. Punishment. A client fish that gets bitten instead of cleaned can chase the cleaner or leave. Cleaner wrasses that cheat are punished, and they learn. Reputation. In experiments, cleaner fish behaved more honestly when other clients were watching, as if they understood that image matters. A fish. Managing its brand. Partner choice. Clients choose which cleaners to visit. Cleaners compete for clients. Economists would call it a market, and in 1994 the biologists Ronald Noe and Peter Hammerstein formalized exactly that idea: a biological market, where partners compete to be chosen and the price of service floats with supply and demand. Cost of exit. If the cleaning stops, the parasite load returns. Everyone in the system has skin in the game, sometimes literally. None of this involves love. None of it needs to. 7/ The counterfeit If a trade works, someone will fake it. Nature learned that lesson before banks did. On Indo-Pacific reefs, the cleaner wrasse has a doppelganger: a small fish called the sabre-toothed blenny. It copies the cleaner's colors, its stripe, even its dance, the little rocking motion that tells clients, "Hold still, it is safe." Large fish, trained by thousands of honest interactions, relax and open up. Then the blenny bites out a chunk of fin or skin and vanishes. That is not a glitch. That is parasitism wearing the uniform of a partnership, and it only works because the real partnership is so reliable. Think about what that implies. The more honest the system, the more profitable the lie. A counterfeit is worthless in a world with no real currency. It becomes valuable the moment everyone trusts the genuine article. Hosts fight back, and the arms race is exactly what you would predict. Clients learn to spot tells. They approach more cautiously when a cleaner is unfamiliar. They remember which stations treat them well and which leave scars. Cleaners, in turn, invest in markers that are costly to fake: consistency, location, a fixed spot that clients return to and vouch for with their repeated visits. Reliability is a signal. Showing up in the same place at the same time, with the same behavior, day after day, is the single hardest thing to counterfeit. It also explains something that confuses people about animal trust. Trust in the wild is rarely warm. It is a running tally. An animal that has been cleaned without incident a hundred times has a hundred pieces of evidence. One incident erases most of them. Nature's version of a credit score updates in real time, and the penalty for default is a bite. So when you watch two animals that should be enemies sharing the same patch of dirt, do not ask whether they like each other. Ask how many times they have done this before. 8/ The price of lying still Now, the question I promised you would matter in two minutes. Every mutualism has a hidden bill, and it is rarely paid in food. It is paid in vulnerability. Look at what the host must do to be cleaned. It has to stop. Not walk, not graze, not scan the horizon every few seconds like a nervous accountant. It has to hold still, and hold still for a long time, because tick removal is not a quick job. It has to let something else take over its attention. A groomed animal is a distracted animal. Primatologists have measured that some primates spend up to a fifth of their waking hours grooming each other. Robin Dunbar argued that this is not about hygiene at all, that grooming is how social animals build the trust that group living runs on. It is a currency. The hours are the price. It has to let its body go quiet. Muscles relax, breathing slows, the animal's usual wariness drops a few notches. Cleaning is a mild trance, and a mild trance on open ground is a risk. And the savanna does not offer discounts to the relaxed. This is the real genius of the trade, and the reason I find it unsettling. The cleaner is not only providing hygiene. If the cleaner is part of a group, it is quietly providing something the host has just given up: lookouts. Banded mongooses have an alarm system. Sentinels, a cry that means a bird of prey, a different cry for something on the ground. One animal sees danger and the whole group knows within a second. A host sitting among them is borrowing an early-warning system for the price of a few hundred ticks. One service, two benefits. The host gets cleaned and gets guards. The mongooses get a meal and a big, formidable, venom-proof neighbor who is not on their menu. It is a mutual-defense treaty, signed through the digestive system. But there is a catch, and the catch is why this works as a story and not just as a fact: The system only holds while everybody's incentives point the same direction. Change one number, and the deal inverts. What happens when the danger is bigger than the deal? What does a small animal owe a large one when something much larger than both arrives? Who stays? Who leaves? Who decides? I will not answer that here. The video does. 9/ Nature does not run on tenderness I want to push back on the way this kind of story usually gets told. You will see it described as friendship, as an inter-species hug, as nature being kind. The comment sections will fill with hearts. It is not kindness. It is better than kindness. It is trade. The mongoose is not being generous. It is eating. The badger is not being grateful. It is being maintained. No one in the transaction is sacrificing anything they do not get back. That is exactly why it is stable. Altruism collapses when the cost gets too high. Self-interest scales. The most reliable cooperation in nature has no love in it. If that makes it feel colder to you, consider the alternative: any arrangement that relies on gratitude, loyalty or good intentions has to be rebuilt every generation. An arrangement that relies on incentives writes itself into the genes. And notice the quiet inversion, the one most people miss: the strongest animal in the story is not the independent one. It is the one that depends. Not because it is weak. Because strength has a blind spot, and every blind spot is a market. Power does not erase needs. It changes their shape. The lion can take what it wants and still cannot remove one tick from the back of its own neck. The honey badger can destroy a snake, a hive, a fence, and cannot reach between its own shoulder blades. You can be undefeated and still be dependent. In fact, the more complete your defenses, the more precisely you can locate the single place where you need someone else. 10/ You live inside the same contract If you think this is a quirk of African wildlife, look inward. Your body carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells, the better part of forty trillion by one widely cited estimate. They digest what you cannot, produce vitamins you cannot make, train your immune system, and keep dangerous microbes from moving in. You provide the warmth and the food. They provide the labor. Nobody has ever voted on it. Deeper still: the mitochondria in every cell of your body, the structures that make most of your energy, were once free-living bacteria. Around one and a half to two billion years ago, one cell swallowed another and, instead of digesting it, struck a deal. Biologist Lynn Margulis spent years being laughed at for proposing this. She turned out to be right. You are, at the cellular level, a merger that never dissolved. Leaf-cutter ants have been farming fungus for roughly fifty million years, long before humans invented agriculture, and the fungus cannot survive without the ants. Clownfish live among anemone tentacles that would kill almost anything else. Lichens, the crusty patches on old stone, are not single organisms at all. They are a fungus and an alga that figured out, a very long time ago, that two incomplete things can make one complete thing. And here is my favorite, because it involves us. In East Africa there is a bird called the greater honeyguide. It leads humans to wild bees' nests. The humans open the hive, take the honey, and leave the wax, which the bird eats. A 2016 study in the journal Science showed that the Yao honey-hunters of Mozambique use a special call, a trilled "brrr-hm," to recruit the birds, and that the call roughly doubled the chance of being guided and sharply increased the chance of reaching a nest. The bird and the human are communicating, and the language was never written down. Folklore says the honeyguide also leads honey badgers to hives. That claim has never been rigorously confirmed, and scientists treat it as a story. But think about why the story exists at all. Because it feels right. Because everyone who has watched this animal for long enough senses the same thing: the toughest animal on the savanna spends its life in a web of arrangements it did not choose and cannot escape. The web is the real organism. The animals are just where it touches the ground. 11/ Why hunters hate alliances Every predator on that savanna runs the same business: surprise. A lion does not win by being faster than a gazelle. It wins by closing the distance before the gazelle knows the distance exists. Cover, wind direction, patience, the long belly-down crawl through the grass. The whole hunt is an information trick. Now picture what a network of small, noisy, constantly watching animals does to that trick. It does not stop the predator. It taxes it. Every sentinel is a tripwire. Every alarm call is a bill that arrives before the attack does. This is the part of mutualism that rarely makes the headlines: alliances do not need to defeat the strong. They only need to make the strong pay more than the meal is worth. Big carnivores are brutally economical. A failed hunt burns calories they may not get back for days. When the odds tilt, they walk away. Not because they are afraid, but because the math stopped working. Which is why the weakest members of a system often hold more leverage than they look like they do. Small animals with good eyes are the savanna's smoke detectors. Nobody loves a smoke detector until the night it goes off. 12/ The question you cannot unask Here is what I keep coming back to. We are told that nature is a contest. Strongest wins. Fastest eats. Weakest feeds the rest. That is true on certain days, in certain frames, under certain cameras. But if the contest were the whole story, the savanna would be empty. Every animal on it would be an isolated fortress, slowly bleeding from wounds it cannot reach. The reason it is full is the other half of the story: arrangements. Quiet, unglamorous, cold-blooded, mutually profitable arrangements between creatures that have no reason to like each other, and every reason to keep showing up. So the question is not who is the strongest. The question is who needs whom, how badly, for how long, and what happens to the deal the moment the cost changes. Because deals break. They break when the cheater finds out nobody is watching. They break when a bigger threat reshuffles every incentive in a second. They break when one side decides that survival outranks the contract. And that is the moment I want you to watch for. Not the part everyone will talk about. Not the part with the loudest reaction. The part where the incentives flip. 13/ Before you press play Do me a favor. Do it once, then do it again. First time, watch it like everyone else. Let it happen. Feel whatever you feel. Second time, watch with one rule: ignore the loudest animal. Track the quiet ones. Notice who looks where. Notice who moves first. Notice who does not move at all. Notice what each animal does with its body, not its face. You will find a negotiation hiding in plain sight. No words. No signatures. Just bodies, incentives and time. Then ask yourself the question I cannot stop asking: If you were the one lying in the dirt, who would you trust to watch your back? And more importantly: Who in your own life has been quietly cleaning something off yours, while you pretended you did not need it? The best partnerships in nature were never sentimental. They were just honest about what each side wanted. Maybe that is the lesson. Maybe that is also the problem. One last thing. The reason footage like this spreads has little to do with the animals. Every viewer quietly runs the same calculation: who is protecting whom, who is using whom, and what would I do in that spot. You are not watching nature. You are watching a mirror with fur. And the mirror is asking about your deals. Save this thread now. After the second watch, you will read it very differently, and the lines that felt like commentary will start to feel like clues. Play the video. Watch to the final second. Then tell me who you think blinked first.

$NOW   Q3 2026: The Demand Is Real, but the "Perfect Setup" Just Broke   The market wanted perfection. It got a fundamentally strong beat, but an 18% pre-market haircut. Why? Because after a 66% YTD run fueled by the AI narrative, expectations were flawless. The 18% drop isn't about demand collapsing—it. It's a brutal valuation reset triggered by decelerating cRPO guidance and accounting optics.  The underlying business is firing on all cylinders: $5M+ net new ACV deals surged 135% YoY to 19 deals, and the annual AI ACV target was raised to $1.7B. But the stock is now paying the price for a compressed margin profile and cautious Q4 guidance.  1. Why the 18% Drop? The "Triple Whammy" of Optics  If deals are surging, why did GAAP net income plummet 45% to $277M and GAAP subscription gross margin fall from 80% to 73.5%?  The M&A Amortization Drag: NOW spent over $10B acquiring Moveworks, Veza, and Armis. The amortization of purchased intangibles hit $198M this quarter, directly hitting COGS. Strip this out, and Non-GAAP subscription gross margin remains a pristine 80%.  ASC 606 Revenue Isolation: To accelerate AI adoption, NOW bundles deployment services with large contracts. Under ASC 606, this revenue is stripped from high-margin subscriptions and dumped into professional services (which runs at a -32.5% gross margin). This dragged subscription growth by ~25 bps and isn't counted in cRPO.  Cloud Bills and Severance: Compute costs to support AI exploded, and the company paid $87M in severance to streamline operations using AI.  The Real Killer (The Guidance): Q3 cRPO came in at $13.65B (+20.5%), actually beating expectations. But management guided Q4 cRPO growth to decelerate to 18.5% (consensus was ~19.8%).   For a SaaS company, the cRPO "bathtub" is the ultimate forward-looking metric. When the inflow is expected to slow, the market panics that new AI ACV isn't yet big enough to offset the normalization of the traditional business cycle.  Furthermore, Non-GAAP EPS was $1.00 (missing the $1.02 consensus), driven by lower interest income and higher debt costs from the Armis deal. Debt-funded M&A is now eating into the bottom line.  2. What Exactly is ServiceNow Selling? (And the client?)  NOW is built on a unified platform (Now Platform) outputting four core workflows: Tech (ITSM, Ops), CRM & Industry, Core Business (HR, Legal, Procurement), and Creator (App Engine/Low-code).  They sell to the absolute top of the food chain. Out of 8,800 customers, roughly 90% are Fortune 500. They now have 680 "super-users" with ACV > $5M (+23% YoY). A 98% renewal rate is the ultimate safety net.  The Pricing Pivot: From "Seats" to "Consumption"  The classic SaaS "seat-based" pricing is facing an existential threat in the AI era—if AI reduces human headcount, seat revenue shrinks. NOW is smoothly transitioning to a hybrid model: locking in the base platform by headcount, but charging for AI Agent tasks and compute usage (Pro Plus bundles and consumption).  Crucially, non-seat-based revenue now accounts for nearly 50% of new ACV. This is the holy grail for SaaS companies trying to survive the AI transition.  3. Trump knew. He blew it off because he was making money.  Trump was briefed last year about an alleged Chinese intelligence asset cultivating a relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. U.S. intelligence reportedly concluded she was funneling information to Beijing.  But here’s what makes this even more troubling. The Commerce Department had already been investigating Megaspeed since late 2024, under Biden, after officials found Nvidia equipment sitting in boxes at a Malaysian data center, raising suspicions about potential diversion to China.  U.S. officials communicated their concerns about Megaspeed to Singaporean and Malaysian authorities, as well as Nvidia. The investigation was already underway before Trump took office.  We don’t yet know whether the Biden administration knew about the alleged espionage specifically. But the warning signs surrounding the company and its access to advanced AI chips were already there.  Then Trump was briefed on the intelligence. According to the New York Times, he took no action amid concerns about disrupting Nvidia’s chip sales, economic growth and the stock market, and complicating trade relations with China.  And the administration did nothing to warn Huang.  While the alleged threat remained, Nvidia contributed at least $20 million toward Trump’s ballroom fund, according to a source familiar with the donation who spoke to the Times.  When national security collides with personal profits and political relationships, Americans deserve to know the facts.

I asked Google AI why this matter was not referred for Military Tribunal under the U.C.M.J. and to the DoJ instead. What I learned may be interesting to some of you.  Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was fired from his post as the Joint Staff’s top military planner (J5) by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth following an internal investigation into allegations that he leaked classified information regarding the Iran and Russia-Ukraine wars to journalists.  The decision to refer the case to the Department of Justice (DOJ) rather than immediately pursuing a military court-martial stems from several legal, jurisdictional, and procedural factors:  1. Jurisdictional Authority Over Leaks-  The unauthorized disclosure of national defense information is a federal crime governed by civilian statutes, primarily the Espionage Act (18 U.S.C. § 793). Because the case involves classified intelligence, meetings with civilian journalists outside the Pentagon, and broader national security implications, the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the FBI hold the primary investigative and prosecutorial mandate for federal crimes of this scale.   2. Immediate Removal vs. Legal Process-  A court-martial is a lengthy, formal trial process under the Uniform Code of Military Justice (UCMJ). Because the leaks were deemed an active threat to national security, Secretary Hegseth took immediate administrative action to strip him of his authority and access. Following his ouster, reports indicate that Sylvia is retiring from the military. Once a service member separates or transitions out of active duty status, pursuing civilian federal charges via the DOJ is often more straightforward than holding a military tribunal.   3. Handling Classified Evidence (CIPA)-  Prosecuting high-level classified leaks requires strict protocols for protecting state secrets during a trial. Civilian federal courts utilize the Classified Information Procedures Act (CIPA), which provides a highly refined legal framework for judges to determine how classified evidence can be introduced without further compromising national security.  4. Broad Scope Involving Civilians-  Because the investigation involves civilians (the journalists he allegedly met with outside of military installations), a military court-martial would lack the jurisdiction to subpoena or investigate those civilian entities. The DOJ possesses the cross-jurisdictional authority required to conduct an investigation involving both military personnel and civilian targets.  Current Status-  While the DOJ handles the criminal investigation into the underlying disclosures, the military retains the right to pursue separate UCMJ actions if it chooses, though high-profile national security leak cases are traditionally deferred to federal civilian prosecution."

🇯🇵 🚨 UPDATE: YMIRLINK CUENOTE BREACH GROWS TO 49 SYSTEMS AND 51.6M RECORDS  Japan's Ymirlink has published a second report on the attack on its Cuenote FC email-delivery service. Data output is now confirmed on 49 Cuenote FC systems, with 51,628,280 cumulative records possibly exposed, up from about 9 million across five systems in the Oct 19 first report.  What the Oct 26 report adds: • A retroactive log review found 42 more affected systems on Oct 25; Ymirlink says it contacted those 42 client companies by 12:30 JST on Oct 26 • The attackers also read data across systems through the planted program and hijacked login sessions • 16 systems are still being counted, so the total may rise • Its Cuenote BASE customer system left 190 client-contact records viewable (company, name, phone, email) • Scam emails spoofing a card brand from a cuenote.jp address have been seen  JR Central, JR West and JR Kyushu said on Oct 26 that email addresses, member IDs and names of some Express Reservation and smartEX members were exposed through the service, and they stopped using it. They say their own reservation systems were not breached.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: 51.6M is a cumulative record count, not unique people, and exposed fields differ by client. 🤖🚨 ANTHROPIC: UNRELEASED CLAUDE MODEL WROTE WORKING EXPLOIT CHAINS FOR CHROME, SAFARI, ANDROID, WINDOWS AND LINUX  Anthropic's Frontier Red Team published research on Oct 27, 2026 detailing five attack chains that an unreleased internal Claude research model built after initial prompting, against some of the world's most widely used software.  The five demonstrations: • Chrome: one-click code execution outside the browser sandbox (V8 heap bug, CacheStorage race, FedCM use-after-free) • Safari: one-click chain that bypassed the same-origin policy to read history, cookies and other sites' data • Android: photos and personal data pulled from a locked Pixel 9 over USB without unlocking it • Windows: remote crash of machines serving native HTTP/3 via a kernel QUIC bug (CVE-2026-33096) • Linux: zero-click remote root on servers with a multipath TCP listener (CVE-2026-98432)  Anthropic says every flaw was reported and fixed, including 62 Chrome CVEs patched as of Chrome 156. Google's Chrome release notes and Apple's security advisory credit Anthropic researchers working with Claude.  ⚠️ Analyst Note: These are vendor-reported demonstrations of already-fixed flaws, not an in-the-wild campaign. No in-the-wild exploitation has been verified, and the chains have not been independently reproduced end to end. Keep browsers, phones and kernels patched: AI is shrinking the time from bug to working exploit.  Primary: anthropic.com/research/disco… #DDW #AI #CyberSecurity #Anthropic #VulnerabilityResearch

One interesting implication of WESP is how much control Microsoft will have over EDR telemetry collection on Windows.  Instead of every vendor relying entirely on its own kernel driver, WESP introduces a Microsoft-maintained driver that collects and exposes events through a common interface.  From a telemetry perspective, this could mean:  - More consistent event sources between EDR vendors 👍 - Greater dependence on what Microsoft chooses to expose 👎  (𝘔𝘪𝘤𝘳𝘰𝘴𝘰𝘧𝘵 𝘥𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘴 𝘸𝘩𝘪𝘤𝘩 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘴 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘧𝘪𝘦𝘭𝘥𝘴 𝘦𝘹𝘪𝘴𝘵 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘧𝘪𝘳𝘴𝘵 𝘱𝘭𝘢𝘤𝘦) - More emphasis on vendor filtering, enrichment, and additional telemetry sources 👍  Of course, this depends on adoption and how complete WESP becomes. Vendors may still need their own drivers for capabilities it doesn't support.  I think raw events will start to look the same across vendors, assuming that vendors will collect and enrich the raw events provided by WESP (I doubt many will do that).  Very interesting development for anyone that cares about EDR telemetry though...  @zodiacon's analysis: elastic.co/security-labs/blo…

🚨 WordPress 7.1.4 released with fixes for 22 security vulnerabilities WordPress has released version 7.1.4 and is urging administrators to update their websites immediately. ⠀ The security release addresses a race condition in the core upgrade process that could lead to remote code execution during the upgrade window. It also fixes multiple stored cross-site scripting vulnerabilities affecting block markup, privacy data removal requests, the Interactivity API, Customizer selective refresh, Categories, playlists, images, comment pagination and specially crafted usernames. ⠀ Other resolved issues include: • Disclosure of unpublished Customizer changes to unauthenticated visitors • A stored denial-of-service issue in the Interactivity API • Improper access to Notes attached to posts • Several security-hardening weaknesses • Replacement of bundled root certificates following the eMudhra revocation ⠀ Many of the vulnerabilities require Contributor, Author or Editor-level access, but the exact requirements vary by issue. Security fixes have also been released for affected branches from WordPress 7.0 through 4.7. Versions 4.6 and earlier no longer receive security updates. ⠀ WordPress has not indicated that any of the vulnerabilities are being actively exploited. Administrators can install the update through Dashboard > Updates. Sites with automatic background updates enabled should begin updating automatically. Source: https:// wordpress.org/news/2026/10/wor dpress-7-1-4/

🚨🇺🇸 Discord will let search engines index messages from public servers Starting in mid-December, messages posted in eligible public channels on Discoverable Discord servers may appear on server web pages and in search results on Google and other search engines. ⠀ The change only applies to Discoverable Servers, which have at least 1,000 members and can be joined without an invitation. Private servers, restricted channels, direct messages and group DMs are excluded. ⠀ Discord says: • Messages posted before the rollout will not be included • Usernames and avatars will not appear beside indexed messages • Participating channels will be clearly labeled • Server administrators can exclude individual channels or disable the feature • Users can prevent future messages from appearing through Data & Privacy settings • Teen accounts are excluded entirely ⠀ The individual message setting will be enabled by default in most regions. It will be disabled by default in the EU/EEA, UK, Canada, Brazil, Australia and South Korea. Turning the setting off only affects messages posted while it is disabled. Messages sent while the feature was enabled may remain public unless the original Discord message is deleted, and cached search results may take longer to disappear. ⠀ Beginning November 16, every Discoverable Server will also receive a public Server Web Page that may contain AI-generated summaries of discussions from selected public channels. Source: https:// discord.com/blog/making-conten t-from-discoverable-servers-easier-to-discover

🚨🇦🇪 Telegram zero-day can enable code execution through malicious animated content A vulnerability in Telegram’s rlottie animation library can allow attackers to execute arbitrary code within the application process. Tracked as CVE-2026-111105, the flaw carries a CVSS score of 7.0 and was publicly disclosed by Trend Micro’s Zero Day Initiative after remaining unresolved at the client-code level. ⠀ The vulnerability is caused by improper validation of attacker-controlled animation data, resulting in a write before the beginning of an allocated memory buffer. ⠀ Despite reports describing the flaw as a zero-click sticker attack, ZDI’s final advisory says user interaction is required. The victim must visit a malicious page or open a malicious file for exploitation to occur. ⠀ Telegram told ZDI that server-side sticker validation mitigates the vulnerability. However, ZDI continued seeking a client-side fix and ultimately published the issue as a zero-day advisory on October 15. ⠀ No affected client versions, patched versions or confirmed in-the-wild attacks have been disclosed. Users should keep Telegram updated and avoid opening untrusted animated files, sticker packs or external links until a client-side fix is confirmed. Source: https://www. zerodayinitiative.com/advisori es/ZDI-26-757/

sample_texts: A year ago, MIT took down a paper, sponsored by an AI cyber vendor, saying 80% of ransomware attacks

sample_tweets.text:
A year ago, MIT took down a paper, sponsored by an AI cyber vendor, saying 80% of ransomware attacks use GenAI.  It was total bullshit.  They said they would urgently reviewing it before restoring it.

A year later: it never returned.  They just pretended it never happened.
oh I know, it's not a critique of you.  We're, what, 4 years into the GenAI thing now. I think by year 10 the real story will be the harm caused by security leaders during this period.

There are people in the industry who realise all this btw, but they're essentially drowned out by well meaning folks who are repeating groupthink and panic.  

There's 100% a diversity of thought issue in cybersecurity, and misaligned incentives.  The real GenAI exploit has been of people.

If you ask any major cyber insurance provider they'll tell you they aren't getting claims for AI incidents.  They're getting the same claims for foundational security issues that orgs never solved.

Organisations pushing out diversity initiatives is shameful, as is the direction of travel of cyber.

The cybersecurity industry needs to calm down.  There is no cyber AI apocalypse.  There is a lot of crying wolf.  

The ratio of vulns to CISA KEVs (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities) actually went down last year, and continues to be super low.

The clamour for budget and money will backfire.
I ain't.

### 1. 현재 주요 사이버보안 트렌드
최근 사이버 위협은 웹 백엔드 런타임 취약점(PHP, Node.js)을 악용한 RCE 공격과 AI 에이전트 및 모델의 보안 취약점을 노리는 공격이 핵심입니다. 특히 `PHP2Shell` 및 `Node2Shell`과 같은 취약점이 실제 인프라 공격에 활발히 연쇄적으로 악용되고 있으며, 공격자들은 AI 도구를 활용해 보안 탐지를 우회하거나 개발자 워크스테이션을 클라우드 침투의 교두보로 삼고 있습니다([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/96187/)). 또한, 미군 기지의 냉장고 오작동 사례처럼 사물인터넷(IoT) 기기를 대상으로 한 사이버 공격 의심 사례가 보고되는 등 공격 표면이 물리적 인프라까지 확장되는 추세입니다([TheHackerNews](https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/telegram-android-flaw-lets-attackers.html)).

### 2. 주요 위협 행위자 / 캠페인
- **TAG-217**: 한국 금융권을 대상으로 AI 기반 프레임워크인 `ARTEX`를 사용하여 공격을 수행함([Recorded Future](https://www.recordedfuture.com/blog/tag-217-artex-south-korean-banks)).
- **GhostAction**: 개발자 엔드포인트와 클라우드 액세스를 노리는 공급망 공격 캠페인을 지속 중([DarkReading](https://www.darkreading.com/application-security/ghostaction-hacking-wave-fizzles-attackers-github)).
- **Unknown APT**: 아시아 정부용으로 커스터마이징된 Windows 10 OS를 대상으로 `NetamLoader`를 사용하는 정교한 타겟 공격 수행([Securelist](https://securelist.com/netamloader/121676/)).

### 3. 한국 관련 위협
- **개인정보 유출 사고**: SK플래닛 기프티콘(쿠폰 일련번호 및 환급계좌 포함), 빗썸(고객 및 임직원 주민번호/신분증 사본 포함), 한국전력공사(퇴직자 정보 추가 유출) 등 대규모 개인정보 유출 사고 발생([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=209175)).
- **금융권 위협**: TAG-217에 의한 한국 금융권 타겟 공격 및 국내 금융권 대상 Phishing/Infostealer 악성코드 유포 지속([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/96154/)).

### 4. 주요 CVE / 취약점
1. **CVE-2026-98432**: Linux Kernel IPv4 TCP/multipath UAF 취약점, CVSS 9.8(Critical), 원격 코드 실행 가능([Ubuntu Security](https://ubuntu.com/security/CVE-2026-98432)).
2. **CVE-2026-109618 / 109619**: PHP RCE 취약점(`PHP2Shell`), Critical, 활발히 악용 중([Unit42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/)).
3. **CVE-2026-111497**: Node.js Brotli 디코더 RCE 취약점(`Node2Shell`), Critical, 패치 권고([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/96266/)).
4. **CVE-2026-110264**: GitLab 정규 표현식 컴파일러 RCE 취약점, Critical, 긴급 패치 배포([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5787)).
5. **CVE-2026-91403**: Oracle Java JSSE 인증서 검증 우회 취약점, Critical, 긴급 업데이트 권고([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5789)).

### 5. IOC 요약
- **CVE**: 
    - CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619 ([Unit42](https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2026-109618-cve-2026-109619/))
    - CVE-2026-111497 ([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/96266/))
    - CVE-2026-110264 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5787))
    - CVE-2026-91403 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5789))
- **도메인/해시**: 이번 수집 데이터 내 특정 도메인 및 해시값은 보안상 직접 나열하지 않음 (상세 보고서 참조 권장).

### 6. 즉각 대응 권고
- **패치 적용**: PHP, Node.js, GitLab, Java 등 웹 백엔드 런타임의 최신 보안 업데이트를 즉시 적용하여 `PHP2Shell`, `Node2Shell` 공격 차단.
- **접점 보안 강화**: 외부 노출된 웹 서비스, API, 위탁 SaaS의 접근 제어를 강화하고, 특히 관리자 페이지에 대한 인증 강화 및 모니터링 수행.
- **공급망 및 권한 관리**: 개발자 워크스테이션의 보안을 강화하고, 불필요한 권한(예: `SeManageVolumePrivilege`) 할당 여부를 점검하여 권한 상승 공격 방지.

### 7. 위협 수준 평가
- **점수**: 9/10
- **근거**: Critical 등급의 RCE 취약점이 다수 공개되었고, 국내 주요 기업을 대상으로 한 실질적인 대규모 개인정보 유출 사고가 동시다발적으로 발생함.
